newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 3.

text.p: More than 2200 pupils have been suspended in the first nine weeks of the school year, 458 of them for drug abuse. Figures disclosed by the Education Ministry on Wednesday show that so far this year 2226 pupils, mainly secondary school but some intermediate, have been suspended -- an average of 247 a week. Page 1.

Senior Government Whip John Carter owned up on Wednesday to spending $40,000 to $50,000 a year in airfares for travel between his Northland electorate and Wellington. His disclosure -- on the eve of today's government administration select committee meeting where ACT NZ's perk-buster Rodney Hide has said he will grill Parliamentary Services Commission officials on MPs' expenses -- comes a day after Labour MP Jonathan Hunt admitted running up a $29,170 taxi bill in the year to June 30 1996. Page 1.

Parliament's privileges committee has all but finalised its verdict on the contempt charge against Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, Attorney-General Paul East said on Wednesday night. "I am certainly not going to disclose the conclusions of the committee but I'm hopeful that we will not be required to meet again on the matter and we'll be able to report to Parliament when Parliament resumes," he said. Page 1.

A trip to Hawaii was paid for NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan by the Maori health trust which helped him get his car. Raukura Hauora O Tainui Trust chairman Taitimu Maipi on Wednesday confirmed last December's three-day trip was payment for part-time public relations consultancy work Morgan did for the trust in May. Maipi was reported on Wednesday saying the airfare and accommodation cost $1200. Page 2.

Labour leader Helen Clark has ruled out any shift to the left in the party's policies, but says Labour will need Alliance support to succeed at the next election. "There would be absolutely no point in Labour moving further towards the Alliance's policies, because there is no market. The election showed that," she said. Page 2.

The Fish and Game Council said on Wednesday that Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission chairman Sir Tipene O'Regan was trying to scare the Crown out of appealing against the recent controversial court ruling on trout fishing. District
court-judge Andrew Becroft gave Maoris the right to fish trout without a licence in tribal areas. Page 2.

The Business Roundtable, Council of Trade Unions and the Manufacturers Federation were united on Wednesday in their opposition to the government's economic policies outlined in the Budget Policy Statement. The three organisations, traditionally opponents themselves, told Parliament's finance and expenditure select committee that the statement's goals were wrongly focused at the better-off and had little to offer lower-income families. Page 2.

The government would have to make $3.2 billion in tax cuts over the next five years to offset the cost to taxpayers of introducing compulsory superannuation savings, Council of Trade Unions economist Peter Harris said on Wednesday. The figure -- which includes $1.1 billion in planned tax cuts next year -- would leave the government having to make cuts in spending, Harris said. Page 2.

Cut parliamentary perks, but boost MPs salaries, says National MP Christine Fletcher. She is supporting a compaign by ACT NZ's Rodney Hide to have MPs bulk funded and said the debate had to look at the real costs on MPs. Fletcher said the Higher Salaries Commission had been told to put the breaks on MPs' salaries, and as a result perks had been used by way of compensation. Page 2.

The kiwi icecream icon, Tip Top, has fallen into Australian hands. Heinz Wattie has sold the Tip Top Ice Cream division to diversified Western Australian food comopany Peters and Brownes for an undisclosed sum. Earlier estimates had put a price tag of $300 million to $350 million on Tip top. Final settlement is expected in mid to late April. Page 12.

New Zealand's two largest insurance groups will be going head to head in the phone banking business after the launch on Wednesday of National Mutual's Freedom Financial Services. Freedom will compete with rival insurer AMP Group's telephone
banking subsidiary, Ergo Personal Financial Services, which offers a wide range of home loans and savings and investment products over the phone. Page 12.

Seven years after DFC collapsed, its statutory managment has announced it will pay no interest on $1.1 billion of tier-2 debt as at April 15. When the company collapsed in 1989, creditors were divided into three groups or tiers, with tier-1 creditors repaid in full in April 1992. The statutory managers said they expected surplus funds would be paid out as interest on October 15, when the full $1.1 billion in the tier-2 debt would be repaid. They advised on Wednesday than "no interest will be paid on DFC's tier-2 debt as at April 15, 1997". Page 12.

Seven key economic ministers will front up to 200 people from companies, trade groups and other organisations at a summit behind closed doors in Wellington today. Business leaders may raise concerns about the Coalition's cohesion and its ability to govern, state spending and issues like compliance costs and ACC levies. Only the speech by Prime Minister Jim Bolger and the closing address by Employers Federation president Simon Holdsworth will be open to the media. Page 12.

Taking the axe to business development boards is one Commerce Ministry option put to Business Development Minister Max Bradford. Papers sent to Bradford last December and made public through Parliament's commerce select committee last week, offer three options for the boards' future. These are rationalising the current 21 into three or one, a takeover by the ministry, and abolition. Page 12.
